To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the mammary gland is able to increase milk protein yield by adjusting local conditions, including increasing blood flow and extraction efficiency of amino acids, to maintain an adequate supply of nutrients for protein synthesis.

the mammary gland is capable of adjusting its amino acid uptake and utilization to support the increased demand of milk protein production, and the increased demand for milk protein is achieved by increasing the extraction efficiency of amino acids and glucose, increasing mammary blood flow and glucose uptake, and maintaining a positive mammary nitrogen and carbon balance.

the mammary gland is capable of maintaining a positive balance of total amino and carbon nitrogen during a hyperinsulinemia-euglycemia, and that the ability to increase mammary extraction of essential amino acids and increase mammary blood flow are important adaptations that allow the mammary gland of the lactating cow to maintain milk protein synthesis during a hyperinsuline-mia-euglycema.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of milk protein yield.
the effects of insulin on the mammary gland.
the regulation of mammary protein synthesis and the effects of insulin on the utilization of amino acids by this tissue.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in the presence of an adequate supply of essential amino acids and insulin, the mammary mammary gland has the ability to increase milk protein production by increasing its extraction efficiency of essential branched-chain amino acid, by increasing blood flow to the gland, and by increasing its uptake of glucose.

the insulin-induced increases in milk protein yields were due to increased extraction efficiency of essential and nonessential amino acids, increased mammary blood flow and glucose uptake, and increased efficiency of glucose utilization by the mammary epithelial cells.
insulin and postruminally supplied amino acids are not the primary determinants of milk protein yield.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
insulin is an important regulator of mammary gland metabolism and that the mammary gland has a unique ability to adjust to changing nutrient supply.

insulin increases the uptake and utilization of amino acids by mammary tissue for milk protein synthesis, and that the increased uptake is achieved by an increase in blood flow and extraction efficiency of amino acids.
the mammary gland is capable of using amino acids from the blood to support milk protein synthesis, and this utilization is regulated in response to changes in supply.
The main takeaway from our work is that
insulin is an important regulator of amino acid metabolism and utilization in the lactating mammary gland, which is a key organ of amino acid metabolism.
, in the dairy cow, the mammary epithelial cells are able to increase their efficiency of amino acid utilization for milk protein synthesis in response to increased demand.
the mammary gland is able to increase the extraction of amino acids from the blood, and that it does this by increasing mammary blood flow.
